presentingComplaint: Found drowsy and cold at home during a winter cold snap, with progressive lethargy over 2 weeks.
history: Brought in by family after being found obtunded and unarousable at home on a very cold morning. Two-week history of increasing lethargy, cold intolerance, constipation, hoarse voice and reduced appetite. Long-standing primary hypothyroidism on levothyroxine, but admits she stopped taking it ~3 months ago because she 'felt fine'. Prior partial thyroidectomy for goitre. Recent minor chest infection treated with a sedating cough syrup. No focal neurology, no head injury. Risk factors: elderly female, non-adherence to thyroid replacement, cold exposure, intercurrent infection and CNS depressant exposure as precipitants.
examination: Obtunded, arousable only to pain. Dry, coarse, doughy non-pitting skin; periorbital and pretibial puffiness; macroglossia; sparse eyebrows (lateral third loss). Bradycardic, hypothermic, hypoventilating with shallow breaths. Delayed relaxation of ankle reflexes ('hung-up' reflexes). Old transverse cervical thyroidectomy scar. Pertinent negatives: no neck stiffness, no focal deficit, no exophthalmos or tremor, no purpuric rash, no localising signs of sepsis.

labs.Cortisol (random): sent to exclude concomitant adrenal insufficiency
labs.TSH-context: consistent with severe primary hypothyroid decompensation

imaging: CXR: low lung volumes, small pericardial effusion silhouette; no consolidation. ECG: sinus bradycardia, low-voltage complexes, prolonged QT. CT head unremarkable (done to exclude structural cause of coma).
microbiology: Blood and urine cultures sent to exclude precipitating infection; pending. No antimicrobial indicated unless a source is confirmed.
citations: Harrison 22e — Hypothyroidism (Disorders of the Thyroid Gland)
American Thyroid Association Guidelines for Hypothyroidism in Adults 2014
stewardship: Not applicable — non-infective. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics are given only if a precipitating infection is clinically suspected/confirmed; the decompensation itself is endocrine.
contraindications: Aggressive external rewarming can precipitate vasodilatory shock — use passive rewarming
Do not give levothyroxine without first covering with IV hydrocortisone (risk of precipitating adrenal crisis)
Avoid sedatives/opioids which further depress ventilation
Correct hyponatraemia slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination
edgeCases: Precipitating illness (infection, MI, cold exposure, sedatives) is often the trigger and may mask the diagnosis
Concomitant secondary adrenal insufficiency mandates empiric IV hydrocortisone before thyroid hormone
Hypothermia may read as 'afebrile' even in the presence of sepsis; a normal temperature can be relatively high for a myxoedematous patient
expectedMaiK: This is decompensated severe hypothyroidism (myxoedema coma): the triad of altered mentation, hypothermia and a precipitant in a patient with hypothyroidism and very low free T4 with markedly raised TSH. Give IV hydrocortisone first, then IV levothyroxine, support ventilation and rewarm passively, and treat any precipitant.
expectedNextQuestions: Has she been taking her levothyroxine, and when was the last dose?
Any recent infection, new sedative/opioid medication, or cold exposure as a precipitant?
Any history of adrenal insufficiency or steroid use?
expectedInvestigations: Random serum cortisol (exclude adrenal insufficiency) before thyroid replacement
Septic screen (cultures, CXR) to identify precipitant
regressionAssertions: differential must include an alternative cause of coma with hyponatraemia (hyponatremia or metabolic_enceph)
